name: Upgrade in the field
summary: During one life the unit pays to gain something it did not start with: a weapon, a module such as a shield, an aura mast or a detector, passenger seats, more armour, or a whole new form. The price is money, a resource of its own or seconds spent helpless while the part is fitted. The purchase is made on the unit itself, or once at a team building for every unit of that type already out, and it lasts until the unit dies. Unlike a rank it is chosen and paid for, so it answers the fight at hand; unlike a leeched weapon it needs no kill. The levers: who pays, where it can be bought, how long fitting takes, whether options rule each other out for good, and whether the part shows on the model.
counterplay: Read the part: a bought add-on sits on the model, so fight the unit with what its choice left out (one that took the aura mast has no anti-air gun).
Hit it before or during the fitting: until the part is on it is a stock unit, and while fitting it is busy, still or helpless.
Focus the upgraded one: everything it bought dies with it, so its loss costs the enemy more than a stock unit's.
Once it has made a choice that locks the others out, switch to what that choice can't answer.
Go for the place it buys at: hold or destroy the pad, bench or tech building, or raid the income that pays for the parts.
Against a team-wide research, kill the building before the research finishes, or strike before the enemy can afford it.

other_examples.note: The commander buys parts for itself during the match, grouped by where they mount (the back and each arm) and each paid for in mass, energy and build time. Examples are helper drones that build beside it, a personal shield that then drains energy for as long as it runs, a later part that widens that shield, and a missile launcher that a later purchase turns into a short-range nuclear one. Several parts need an earlier one first, so the upgrades form short chains.

sources.title: UEF Armored Command Unit, Supreme Commander Wiki

other_examples.unit: Grenadier Squad weapon upgrades, the Riflemen's BAR and bought Wehrmacht veterancy
other_examples.note: A Grenadier squad in the field pays munitions for a light machine gun or an anti-tank launcher. Each needs free weapon slots, a tech phase and about half a minute to fit, and a squad holds at most two; the machine gun slows the squad a little and the launcher gives up some anti-infantry punch for a way to hurt armour. The American version is bought once at the Barracks and hands every Riflemen squad two automatic rifles and a suppression ability. Wehrmacht veterancy is bought too, at one building, and reaches squads already out as well as new ones.

sources.title: Grenadier Squad, Company of Heroes Wiki
Riflemen Squad, Company of Heroes Wiki

other_examples.note: The morph twist: once a Baneling Nest stands, a Zergling already in the field can be turned into a Baneling, a different unit with a different job, for extra minerals, gas and time. During the change it sits in a cocoon that cannot move and has a small health pool of its own.

sources.title: Baneling (Legacy of the Void), Liquipedia StarCraft II

shooter_analogues.note: In the co-op mode, destroyed robots drop credits and players spend them at stations in their base on stronger weapons, new abilities and canteen buffs. A purchase belongs to one weapon or to the player's class, refunds are only possible while a wave is being set up, and one map adds forward stations that open only between waves.

sources.title: Upgrade Station, Official Team Fortress Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: Glowing benches stand at fixed spots on the island. A player who walks up to one pays building materials (later gold bars) to raise the rarity of the weapon in hand, which improves its stats; some weapons can't be upgraded. The upgrade spots are places on the map, so getting stronger means going there.

The morph twist in a shooter: every alien player hatches as the basic lifeform and opens a menu on a key to evolve into one of four stronger ones or to add traits. The menu marks what the player can't yet afford and shows which abilities the team's commander has unlocked. The pages read are thin on the rules, so this needs a check before use.

player_translation.summary: You buy a stock unit, then put match money into that same unit while you are alive: at a friendly pad you pick one of a few add-ons, wait a few seconds while it is bolted on, and drive off with a part that changes what you can do. The part shows on your model and is lost when you die.
as_user: You earn money by fighting, and instead of saving it all for your next unit you can spend some on the one you are in.

The pick is a read of the match: the anti-air gun because the enemy bought aircraft, the aura mast because your squad fights around you, the passenger bunker because two teammates on foot want a ride.
Fitting takes a few seconds in which you stand still at the pad, so you choose a quiet moment or ask for cover.
On a unit with one bay, the first part you fit rules out the others for this life, so the choice matters.
An upgraded unit carries your savings on its back: you play it with more care, because dying loses the part as well as the unit.
as_target: You see the part on the model and its icon on the nameplate, and you hear the fitting if you are near, so you always know what a unit has bought.
A unit standing at a pad under a fitting effect is still a stock unit and can't move: hit it now.
What it bought tells you what it lacks; bring the unit type its choice can't answer.
Killing an upgraded unit destroys the money spent on it, so it is worth focusing.
teammates: Teammates ask for a part with a ping ('need anti-air', 'need a ride'), and the heavy unit's driver answers by fitting it.
Team parts are bought for others: an aura mast speeds up and mends the teammates around it, and a bunker gives infantry teammates seats and firing ports.
In the team-research twist, one purchase at the team's tech building gives the part to every teammate driving that unit type, at once, wherever they are.
The enemy team shares what it sees ('their heavy took the bunker'), holds or breaks the upgrade pads, and focuses upgraded units together.
controls: The base pattern spends no counted key: E, the universal enter key, pressed on a friendly upgrade pad opens a small wheel of add-ons for your current unit, the mouse picks one, and fitting runs for a few seconds while you stay on the pad.
Leaving the pad before the fitting ends cancels it and gives the money back.
The field-fit twist puts the wheel on Q, a counted key: fit anywhere, but stand still for longer and pay more.
A part with its own gun aims itself at the nearest target in reach, or becomes a seat that a teammate takes with E.
Middle mouse pings a request for a part on a teammate's unit.
feedback: Every add-on is a distinct piece on the model that reads from above (a turret, a mast, a box of firing ports), plus an icon on the nameplate.
Fitting shows sparks, a progress ring and a ratchet sound that nearby enemies hear.
The wheel greys out what you can't afford or have locked out, and names what each pick will rule out.
A team research ends with a short call-out to both teams, and each unit that gains the part flashes once.
The kill feed shows the add-on icon beside the unit, so everyone sees what was lost.
changes_from_rts: An RTS commander pays for a whole army from one purse; here one player pays for one body, so a part must cost clearly less than moving up to the next unit, or nobody buys it.
Fitting has to be short, a few seconds instead of the half minute a squad weapon takes in Company of Heroes, and it must be possible to cancel, because a player who can't act is out of the game.
An RTS add-on gun fires by itself. For a player it either aims itself, as a weapon on an auto-target mount, or it becomes a second seat for a teammate.
Research that upgrades every unit of a type is invisible power in an RTS; here it needs a call-out and a visible change on each model, and there should be few of them.
Parts die with the unit. Match-long upgrades would make early leads grow, which is the snowball risk already noted for ranks.
The morph twist needs a protected or very short change: a helpless cocoon is fine for one unit among a hundred, but it is a free kill when the cocoon is a player.

team_play.notes: The choice of part is a team call: a unit re-arms mid-life to answer what the enemy fields, and the enemy has to adjust its own picks in turn. Parts such as an aura mast or a passenger bunker exist only for teammates, and the team-research twist lets one player's purchase lift everyone on that unit type.

notes: Uses the buy menu and the money the game needs anyway; the new parts are the pad, the add-on wheel and a fitting state.
Each add-on is content for each unit that can take it: a model part, a weapon or effect, an icon and tuning, so the work grows with units times parts.
Networking is light: one or two flags per unit and a timed state, plus cancel and refund cases.
A part can change the hitbox, the silhouette, the seats and the weapons of a live unit, so those systems must accept changes mid-life.
The morph twist is the heaviest: it swaps the whole unit for another while a player is inside it.
Snowballing: the richer player stacks parts and gets richer; prices, one bay per unit and losing parts on death keep it in check.
A stock unit plus a part can beat the next tier for less money unless the part is priced against that tier.
If parts don't rule each other out, a unit can cover all its weaknesses; the Overlord's one-of-three bay is the safe model.
Team-wide research gives power nobody sees coming and helps most the team that is already ahead.
Enemies can only answer a part they can see: every add-on needs its own silhouette and icon.
Too many parts per unit can't be learned; three per bay is about the limit from above.
Research upgrades change numbers or add a button without changing the model unless a visible mark is added.

variants.name: One bay, pick one
variants.summary: The unit has one mounting point and a short list of parts for it, such as a gun, an aura mast or a passenger bunker; the first one bought rules out the others for the rest of its life.

variants.name: Buy a specialist weapon
variants.summary: A few weapon slots take bought specialist weapons, each fitted in seconds and each changing what the unit can hurt, sometimes with a small cost in speed.
variants.seen_in: Company of Heroes Grenadier Squad (machine gun or anti-tank launcher)

variants.name: Team research
variants.summary: One purchase at a team building gives the part to every unit of that type already in the field, as well as to those bought later.
variants.seen_in: Generals Capture Building and Sentry Drone Gun; Company of Heroes BAR upgrade and bought Wehrmacht veterancy

adds_weaknesses.why: Lacks the part until somebody on the team pays for the research, and loses the chance if the building that sells it is destroyed first.

countered_by.why: Saboteurs who shut down or take the building stop the research that every unit of the type is waiting for.
Artillery levels the building that sells the research from beyond its defenders.

variants.name: Mounts and chains
variants.summary: Several mounting points each take one part, later parts need an earlier one, and the strongest draw on the unit's own energy for as long as they run.

variants.name: Upgrade spots on the map
variants.summary: Parts are sold only at a few neutral benches around the map, so getting stronger means going to a place the enemy can watch or hold.
variants.seen_in: Fortnite Upgrade Bench; the forward stations of one Team Fortress 2 Mann vs. Machine map

variants.name: Morph into another form
variants.summary: The unit pays and sits through a short helpless stage to become a different, more specialised unit for the rest of its life; there is no way back.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Zergling into Baneling; Natural Selection 2 alien lifeforms

adds_weaknesses.why: Helpless for a moment while it changes, and it can't change back if the new form turns out to be the wrong answer.

adds_strengths.why: Re-arms or hardens itself mid-life to answer what the enemy fields, without buying a new unit.

adds_weaknesses.why: Stock, it lacks the part it is meant to buy; fitting costs money and seconds of standing still, and every part is lost when it dies.

countered_by.why: Fast flankers catch it at the pad or mid-fitting, while it is still a stock unit that can't move.
Saboteurs take or shut down the pad or tech building it buys its parts at.

open_questions: Will Shamble Frontlines let a living player buy anything for the unit they are in, or only a new unit? If every unit can buy parts at a terminal, that is a game-wide system, and this pattern should then carry only special bays such as the Overlord's one-of-three.
Who pays: the player's own money, a team pool, or can teammates chip in for a part on someone else's unit?
Is a fitted part final for that life, as on the Overlord, or can a pad swap it for a fee?
Where can parts be bought: only at the base, at pads the team holds, at neutral benches, or anywhere for a longer wait? (Recommended: pads the team holds.)
Should team-wide research exist at all when each player buys one unit? (Recommended: very few, each with a call-out and a visible mark on the model.)
The earn-veterancy file asks where ranks that are bought belong. By this file they are the team-research twist: a purchase at a building that reaches units already in the field.

shooter_fit.reason: Buying during a match is native to the game's buy-your-unit economy and already works in shooters (upgrade stations, upgrade benches, evolving aliens), and a bolted-on part reads well from above. It needs exclusive choices and prices set against the next tier to avoid snowballing.
